name: Nepali
speakers: ≈19 million first-language speakers; ≈32 million including second-language speakers
where: Nepal (official language and lingua franca); Sikkim and the Darjeeling–Kalimpong hills of West Bengal, India (a scheduled language of India); southern Bhutan; Nepali communities in Assam, the Gulf, Malaysia, the UK, USA and Australia
tagline: Nepali opens up the Himalaya — from Kathmandu tea shops and trekking trails to Darjeeling and Sikkim — and Nepalis are delighted when a visitor makes the effort.
intro:
**Nepali** (नेपाली *nepāli*) is the national language of Nepal and the common language between its 120-plus ethnic groups — a Newar shopkeeper, a Sherpa guide and a Tharu farmer will talk to each other in Nepali. It is also an official language in Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills of India and is widely spoken in southern Bhutan. Older names you may meet are *Gorkhali* and *Khas kura*.

Nepali is an Indo-Aryan language, a cousin of Hindi, and is written in the same **Devanagari** script. Many words look alike (पानी *pāni* 'water', घर *ghar* 'house'), and many Nepalis understand Hindi from films. But the grammar and the everyday words are quite different: Nepali has **two verbs 'to be'** (हो and छ), an **ergative marker ले** that appears in the past tense, verbs that change for **four levels of respect**, and its own sound system — Nepali keeps many final vowels Hindi drops, pronounces च as *ts*, and merges ब/व and श/ष/स.

Respect is built into the grammar. There are four ways to say 'you': **तँ** *taṃ* (intimate/rude), **तिमी** *timi* (friends, younger people), **तपाईं** *tapāiṃ* (polite default) and **हजुर** *hajur* (very respectful), and the verb changes with each. This course teaches the standard spoken Nepali of **Kathmandu**, using तपाईं by default and तिमी with friends, with the English loanwords Nepalis really use (मोबाइल, बस, अफिस, टिकट…) noted along the way.
romanizationNote: The romanization follows **pronunciation**, not spelling. Plain *a* is the Nepali inherent vowel अ — a short, slightly rounded sound between the u of 'cup' and the o of 'pot' (नमस्ते sounds like 'no-mos-te'); *ā* is the open a of 'father'. Nepali does **not** distinguish long and short i or u in speech, so we write plain *i* and *u* for both इ/ई and उ/ऊ (पानी *pāni*, दूध *dudh*); the alphabet chart alone uses ī ū to tell the letters apart. Likewise श, ष and स all sound like *s* in everyday speech, so words are written with *s* (देश *des*, भाषा *bhāsā*), and ण is written *n*. व is written *b* where it is pronounced b (वर्ष *barsa*, धन्यवाद *dhanyabād*) and *w* where it is pronounced w (स्वागत *swāgat*, हावा *hāwā*). A final *a* is written only where Nepalis actually say it: most nouns drop it (घर *ghar*), but verb forms, words ending in a cluster and little words keep it (छ *chha*, गयो *gayo*, मित्र *mitra*, अब *aba*, तर *tara*). An *h* after a consonant always means a puff of breath (*kh, chh, ṭh, th, ph* and the breathy voiced *gh, jh, ḍh, dh, bh*) — never English 'th' or 'f'. Dots under *ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh* mark retroflex sounds; plain *t d* are dental. *ch chh j jh* are usually pronounced *ts tsh dz dzh* by Nepali speakers. *ṃ* after a vowel means the vowel is nasal (गाउँ *gāuṃ*, तपाईं *tapāiṃ*). *e* and *o* are pure vowels as in Spanish; *ai* and *au* are real glides as in 'eye' and 'cow'.

script.overview:
Nepali is written in **Devanagari**, the same script as Hindi, Marathi and Sanskrit. It is an **abugida**: every consonant letter carries a built-in vowel *a* (pronounced in Nepali as a short, slightly rounded 'uh/o'). क on its own is *ka*. To write another vowel you add a **vowel sign** (मात्रा *mātrā*): का *kā*, कि/की *ki*, कु/कू *ku*, कृ *kri*, के *ke*, कै *kai*, को *ko*, कौ *kau*. Full vowel letters (अ आ इ…) appear only at the start of a word or after another vowel (आउनु *āunu*, भाइ *bhāi*).

Writing runs **left to right**, and the letters hang from a horizontal **headline** (शिरोरेखा). To cancel the inherent vowel you can add a **halanta** (्) under a letter: छन् *chhan*. Nepali uses the halanta more than Hindi does, especially at the end of verb forms — and, importantly, a final letter *without* halanta in a verb is often pronounced with its vowel (गर *gara* 'do!' vs गर् *gar* 'do!' to an intimate). When two consonants meet inside a word they usually join into a **conjunct** (संयुक्ताक्षर): स + त → स्त in नमस्ते.

Nepali schools teach the alphabet as **12 vowels** (स्वरवर्ण, including अं and अः) and **36 consonants** (व्यञ्जनवर्ण) ending with the three compound letters क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ. Nepal also uses its own **Devanagari digits** ०–९ everywhere — on number plates, bus numbers, prices and dates — so learn them early. Nepali does **not** use the dotted (nukta) letters of Hindi/Urdu: 'z' and 'f' sounds in loanwords are written ज and फ (हजार *hajār*, फोन *phon*). The full stop is the vertical bar । (पूर्णविराम).

groups.title: Vowels (स्वर)
groups.note: Each vowel has a full form (used at the start of a word) and a sign (मात्रा) attached to consonants. In speech Nepali has only six basic vowels — a ā i u e o — plus the glides ai and au. इ/ई and उ/ऊ sound the same.

groups.title: Velar consonants (क-वर्ग)
groups.note: Made at the back of the mouth. Each row of the alphabet goes: plain, aspirated, voiced, voiced-aspirated, nasal.

letters.sound: k with NO puff of air, like the k in 'skin'.
letters.strokes: Vertical line, a loop to the left of it, a curved tail to the right; headline last.

letters.sound: k with a strong puff of air, like 'k' in 'kite' said forcefully.
letters.strokes: A small loop joined to a 'व'-like body, then the vertical line.

letters.sound: g as in 'go'.
letters.strokes: A small hook on the left, a vertical line on the right, headline over both.

letters.sound: g followed by a breathy h, as in 'doghouse' said fast.
letters.strokes: A rounded 'u' shape joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: 'ng' as in 'sing'. Never at the start of a word.
letters.strokes: Like ड with a dot to its right.

groups.title: Palatal consonants (च-वर्ग)
groups.note: In Nepali these are usually pronounced as 'ts' sounds (tongue tip behind the teeth): च ts, छ tsh, ज dz, झ dzh. Before i, e and y they sound closer to English ch/j.

letters.sound: Usually 'ts' as in 'cats', without a puff. Before i/e it can sound like 'ch'.
letters.strokes: A short bar from the left joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: 'ts' with a strong puff of air. Also a hugely common word: छ chha 'is' — and the number 6.
letters.strokes: A rounded body with a little curl in the middle, hanging from the headline; no vertical line.

letters.sound: Usually 'dz' as in 'adze'; before i/e closer to English j. Also used for the z of English loans (जु zoo).
letters.strokes: A sideways 'S' curve joined to the vertical line.

letters.sound: 'dz' + breathy h.
letters.strokes: A '3'-like body with a tail, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: 'ny' as in 'canyon'; in practice used before च/ज and pronounced 'n'.
letters.strokes: A curve with a tail and a vertical line.

groups.title: Retroflex consonants (ट-वर्ग)
groups.note: Curl the tongue tip back and touch the roof of the mouth behind the ridge. Between vowels ड and ढ often become a quick flap (like Hindi ड़ ढ़), but Nepali writes them without a dot.

letters.sound: Hard, 'hollow' t with the tongue curled back; no puff. Closest to the English t.
letters.strokes: A curl hanging from the headline, open to the right; no vertical line.

letters.sound: Retroflex t with a puff of air.
letters.strokes: A small circle hanging from the headline.

letters.sound: Retroflex d; between vowels a quick flap.
letters.strokes: Like a 'z' curve hanging from the headline with a dot-less tail.

letters.sound: Retroflex d + breathy h.
letters.strokes: Like ड with a small loop at the bottom.

letters.sound: Spelled as a retroflex n, but most speakers just say 'n'.
letters.strokes: Two little vertical strokes joined by a curve, then a vertical line.

groups.title: Dental consonants (त-वर्ग)
groups.note: Tongue tip pressed against the back of the upper teeth — further forward than English t/d. English speakers' t/d sound retroflex to Nepali ears.

letters.sound: Soft t with the tongue on the teeth, no puff — like French/Spanish t.
letters.strokes: A short curve from the left meeting a vertical line.

letters.sound: Dental t with a puff of air. Never the 'th' of 'thin'.
letters.strokes: A small loop with a curved tail joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: Soft d with the tongue on the teeth.
letters.strokes: A '5'-like curve hanging from the headline, no vertical line.

letters.sound: Dental d + breathy h. Never the 'th' of 'this'.
letters.strokes: A small loop joined to a vertical line; NOTE: no headline over the loop part.

letters.sound: n with the tongue on the teeth.
letters.strokes: A short hooked bar joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: p with no puff of air, as in 'spin'.
letters.strokes: A 'u' shape joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: p with a puff; many speakers soften it towards f. Also used for the f of English loans (फोन phon 'phone').
letters.strokes: Write प and add a small curl to the right of the vertical line.

letters.sound: b as in 'bat'.
letters.strokes: A small triangle-like loop joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: b + breathy h, as in 'clubhouse' said fast.
letters.strokes: A '7'-like hook with a loop, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: m as in 'man'.
letters.strokes: A small loop and a bar joined to a vertical line, headline across.

groups.title: Semivowels (अन्तस्थ)
groups.note: य र ल व. Note that व is usually pronounced b at the start of a word and w after a consonant.

letters.sound: y as in 'yes'.
letters.strokes: A small 'u' with a loop, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: A light tapped r, like the tt in American 'butter' or Spanish 'pero'. Never the English r.
letters.strokes: A small hook hanging from the headline. Before another consonant it becomes a hook above (र्क); after one, a slant below (प्र).

letters.sound: Clear l as in 'leaf' (never the dark l of 'full').
letters.strokes: A loop with a curl, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: Pronounced b at the start of most words (वन ban), w after a consonant (स्वागत swāgat) and between vowels (हावा hāwā).
letters.strokes: Like ब but with an open bottom-left loop (ब has a closed triangle).

groups.title: Sibilants and h (ऊष्म)
groups.note: श, ष and स are three letters for what is, in everyday Nepali, one sound: s. Learn the spellings, but say s.

letters.sound: Spelled 'sh' (तालव्य श) but normally said s; some careful speakers say sh in words like श्री.
letters.strokes: A curl with a small loop and a short bar, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: Spelled as a retroflex 'sh' (मूर्धन्य ष), pronounced s. Only in Sanskrit-derived words.
letters.strokes: Write प and add a diagonal stroke across the 'u'.

letters.sound: s as in 'sun' (दन्त्य स).
letters.strokes: A hook and a small bar joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: A breathy, voiced h. In the middle of a word it is often very weak (बहिनी sounds like 'bo-ini').
letters.strokes: A '5'-like shape with a tail hanging from the headline; no vertical line.

groups.title: Compound letters (क्ष त्र ज्ञ)
groups.note: Nepali children learn these three conjuncts as the last letters of the alphabet: क, ख, ग … स, ह, क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ.

letters.sound: क + ष. At the start of a word said 'chhya/chhe'; in the middle 'kchh'. Not 'ksh' as in Hindi.
letters.strokes: A special shape: a क-like loop with a crossed tail, joined to a vertical line.

letters.sound: त + र: 'tr' with a dental t and tapped r.
letters.strokes: Like त with a slanted stroke cutting the left part.

letters.sound: ज + ञ, but pronounced 'gya' in Nepali.
letters.strokes: A special shape: a ज-like curve fused with a loop, joined to a vertical line.

groups.title: Special marks
groups.note: Signs that nasalize, cancel the inherent vowel or punctuate. Nepali does not use the nukta dot.

letters.sound: Chandrabindu (moon and dot): the vowel is said through the nose, with no n. Very common in Nepali verb endings (छौँ chhauṃ 'we are').
letters.strokes: A small upward crescent with a dot above the headline.

letters.sound: Anusvara (dot). Before a consonant it is the nasal that fits it (संसार sansār); at the end of a word it nasalizes the vowel (तपाईं tapāiṃ). Also replaces ँ when a sign already sits above the line.
letters.strokes: A dot above the headline, at the right of the letter.

letters.sound: Visarga: a short breath after the vowel; inside words it often just lengthens the next consonant (दुःख dukha).
letters.strokes: Two small circles one above the other, like a colon.

letters.sound: Halanta (हलन्त): removes the inherent vowel. At the end of verb forms it tells you NOT to pronounce a final a (छन् chhan 'they are').
letters.strokes: A short slanting stroke under the letter.

letters.sound: 'Eyelash ra': the special half-form of र used before य and sometimes व in Nepali (गर्‍यो garyo 'did').
letters.strokes: A small curved 'eyelash' stroke joined to the following letter.

letters.sound: Purnabiram (पूर्णविराम), the Nepali full stop. Question and exclamation marks are the same as in English.
letters.strokes: A single vertical bar.

letters.sound: The sacred syllable Om, seen on temples, prayer flags and greetings cards.
letters.strokes: A 3-like shape with a tail, topped by a chandrabindu.

groups.title: Common conjuncts (संयुक्ताक्षर)
groups.note: When consonants meet with no vowel between them they fuse. Usually the first letter loses its vertical line (half form); र becomes a hook above (reph) or a slant below; some pairs make special shapes.

ह + र. Note: बाह्र 'twelve' is said 'bāhra'.

groups.title: Devanagari digits
groups.note: Used everywhere in Nepal: prices, bus numbers, number plates, dates, official forms. Western digits are also understood.

letters.sound: शून्य sunya — zero.
एक ek — one.
दुई dui — two.
तीन tin — three.
चार chār — four. Looks like a pretzel / figure-8 with a tail.
पाँच pāṃch — five.
छ chha — six.
सात sāt — seven.
आठ āṭh — eight.
नौ nau — nine.

pronunciation.title: The Nepali 'a': round and dark
pronunciation.body:
The inherent vowel अ is the most frequent sound in Nepali, and it is **not** the a of 'cat' nor quite the 'uh' of Hindi. It is a short vowel made with the mouth slightly rounded, between the u of 'cup' and the o of British 'pot'. नमस्ते sounds like 'no-mos-te', कलम like 'ko-lom'. In this course it is written plain *a*.

The contrast that really matters is **a vs ā**: आ is a wide-open 'aa' with unrounded lips. Since Nepali doesn't distinguish long and short i/u in speech, a/ā is the only vowel-length pair you must get right — and it changes meaning constantly: कम *kam* 'less' vs काम *kām* 'work'.
tips: Say English 'cup' with slightly rounded lips — that is roughly अ.
For आ, open your jaw wide as if the doctor said 'say aah'.
Never use the flat 'æ' of 'cat' for either vowel.
Listen for how Nepalis say their own country: नेपाल ne-PAAL, with a clear ā.

pronunciation.title: Final vowels: Nepali keeps more of them
pronunciation.body:
In Hindi the inherent a is dropped at the end of almost every word. Nepali drops it at the end of most **nouns and adjectives** (घर *ghar*, नाम *nām*), but **keeps** it in several big groups of words:

**1. Verb forms**: छ *chha* 'is', गयो *gayo* 'went', गरेन *garena* 'didn't do', गर *gara* 'do!'. When a verb form really ends in a consonant, Nepali spelling marks it with a halanta: छन् *chhan*, गरिन् *garin*, गर् *gar*.
**2. Words ending in a conjunct**: मित्र *mitra*, पत्र *patra*, शब्द *sabda*.
**3. Little words**: अब *aba* 'now', तब *taba*, जब *jaba*, तर *tara* 'but', र *ra* 'and', त *ta*, न *na*, म *ma* 'I'.
**4. Several numbers**: एघार *eghāra* 11, अठार *aṭhāra* 18.

So the same spelling can be read two ways: बस as a noun is *bas* 'bus', but as a command it is *basa* 'sit!'.
tips: If a verb ends without a halanta, say the final a: गर्छ is 'gar-chha', not 'garch'.
Halanta ् at the end = stop on the consonant.
Hindi speakers: अब, तब, कब-type words are 'aba, taba' in Nepali.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration: plain vs breathy consonants
pronunciation.body:
Nepali has plain and aspirated versions of almost every stop. Plain sounds (क त प च ट) have **no** puff of air — like the p in 'spin'. Aspirated ones (ख थ फ छ ठ) have a strong puff. Getting this wrong changes words: दान *dān* 'donation' vs धान *dhān* 'rice paddy'.

The **voiced aspirates** घ झ ढ ध भ are the hardest: a voiced sound followed by breathy murmur, as in 'doghouse', 'madhouse', 'clubhouse' squashed into one syllable. They are frequent in basic words: भात *bhāt* 'rice', घर *ghar* 'house', धन्यवाद *dhanyabād* 'thanks'.

Remember: *th* and *ph* are NOT English 'th' and 'f' — they are a t or p with a puff. (Some Nepalis do soften फ toward f.)
tips: Hold your palm in front of your mouth: still for क त प, a puff for ख थ फ.
For plain p/t/k, think of the sound after s: 'spa, star, sky'.
For bh/dh/gh, start from 'clubhouse, madhouse, doghouse' and shorten.
Don't over-aspirate English-style: Nepali क in काम should feel 'soft'.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental: ट vs त
pronunciation.body:
Nepali has two sets of t/d sounds. **Dental** त थ द ध: tongue tip pressed against the back of your upper front teeth (like French or Spanish t). **Retroflex** ट ठ ड ढ: tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth behind the gum ridge, giving a hollow, 'hard' sound.

English t/d are in between, and Nepalis hear them as retroflex — that's why English loans are written with ट/ड: टिकट *ṭikaṭ* 'ticket', डाक्टर *ḍākṭar* 'doctor'. Your job is mostly to make त/द far enough **forward**.

Between vowels ड and ढ often turn into a quick flap of the curled tongue (गाडी *gāḍi* 'car', पढ्नु *paḍhnu* 'to study'), like Hindi ड़/ढ़; Nepali doesn't write the difference, and neither do we.
tips: For त/द, put your tongue tip literally on your teeth.
For ट/ड, curl the tip back and 'pop' it down.
Practise साथी (friend) vs साठी (sixty) — a mix-up here is a classic learner joke.

pronunciation.title: च छ ज झ: the Nepali 'ts' sounds
pronunciation.body:
In Hindi च and ज are like English ch and j. In native Nepali speech they are usually pronounced further forward, with the tongue tip behind the teeth: **च = ts** (as in 'cats'), **छ = tsh** (ts + puff), **ज = dz** (as in 'adze'), **झ = dzh**. Before i, e and y (चिया *chiyā* 'tea', जेठो *jeṭho* 'eldest') they slide back toward English ch/j. Many speakers in India (Darjeeling, Sikkim) and younger urban speakers use ch/j more.

The romanization keeps *ch chh j jh*, but aim for the ts/dz sounds. Especially notice छ *chha*: it is the most frequent word in the language ('is'), and it sounds like 'tsho', not 'cha'.

As always, keep plain च without a puff and give छ a strong one.
tips: Say 'cats' and keep only the 'ts' — that's च.
छ (is) ≈ 'tsho' with a breath: म ठीक छु ≈ 'ma ṭhik tshu'.
Don't worry if you say English ch/j — you'll be understood; ts/dz just sounds more native.

pronunciation.title: ब and व: one letter, two sounds
pronunciation.body:
Nepali speech has no separate 'v' sound. The letter **व** is pronounced:

**b** at the start of most words: वन *ban* 'forest', वर्ष *barsa* 'year', विद्यार्थी *bidyārthi* 'student', and inside धन्यवाद *dhanyabād*.
**w** after another consonant: स्वागत *swāgat* 'welcome', द्वार *dwār* 'gate', ज्वरो *jwaro* 'fever'; and between vowels: हावा *hāwā* 'wind', नवौँ *nawauṃ* 'ninth'.

So ब and व often sound identical, and many words have both spellings (आइतबार is now standard, but you'll see आइतवार). English 'v' in loans becomes b or bh: भिसा *bhisā* 'visa', भिडियो *bhiḍiyo* 'video'.
tips: Never use an English v sound in Nepali.
Rule of thumb: व at the start = b; व after a consonant or between vowels = w.
When you hear b, it might be spelled ब or व — check the spelling when you learn a word.

pairs.note: Identical in speech: ब=व, ई=इ, ष=स.

pronunciation.title: श ष स — three letters, one 's'
pronunciation.body:
Spelling distinguishes three s-letters, but in everyday Nepali they are all pronounced **s**: देश *des* 'country', भाषा *bhāsā* 'language', सहर *sahar* 'city'. Some educated speakers say 'sh' in a few Sanskrit words (श्री *shri*), and Darjeeling/Sikkim speakers may use more 'sh', but plain s is the Kathmandu norm and always correct.

Two compound letters also surprise learners: **ज्ञ** is 'gya' (ज्ञान *gyān* 'knowledge'), and **क्ष** is 'chhya' at the start of a word and 'kchh' inside (क्षमा *chhyamā* 'forgiveness', शिक्षक *sikchhak* 'teacher'). Neither is the 'ksh/gy' of Hindi.

The flip side: English 'sh' in loanwords is usually s too (शो/सो *so* 'show', मेसिन *mesin* 'machine').
tips: When reading, treat श ष स identically: s.
Learn the spelling separately — it matters for writing exams, not for speaking.
ज्ञ = gya, क्ष = chhya: memorise these two with ज्ञान and क्षमा.

pronunciation.title: No long and short i/u in speech
pronunciation.body:
Devanagari has a 'short' and a 'long' version of i (इ/ई, ि/ी) and u (उ/ऊ, ु/ू). In Hindi the long ones really are longer. **In Nepali they are pronounced the same** — the spelling difference is historical. दिन *din* 'day' and दीन *din* 'humble' are homophones; पानी 'water' ends in an ordinary i.

This is great news for speaking — you have fewer sounds to master — but you must still learn each word's spelling. This course writes plain *i* and *u* for both. The vowel contrast that does matter is **a vs ā** (see 'The Nepali a').

Vowel length in Nepali is controlled by stress and syllable shape instead: vowels before a doubled consonant are short and clipped (पत्ती *patti*), and the first syllable of a word usually carries a little extra weight.
tips: Read ि and ी, ु and ू the same.
Don't lengthen English-style: पानी is 'paa-ni', not 'paa-neee'.
When writing, check the dictionary — spelling mistakes with ि/ी are the most common ones even for Nepalis.

pairs.note: Only the final vowel differs, not the u.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels (ँ and ं)
pronunciation.body:
A **chandrabindu** ँ (or a dot ं above the line) makes a vowel nasal: air goes through the nose as well as the mouth, as in French 'bon', with no n consonant at the end. We write it *ṃ*: गाउँ *gāuṃ* 'village', तपाईं *tapāiṃ* 'you'.

Nasal vowels are everywhere in Nepali grammar: छौँ *chhauṃ* 'we are' vs छौ *chhau* 'you are'; हौँ *hauṃ* 'we are' vs हौ *hau* 'you are'; गरौँ *garauṃ* 'let's do'. Dropping the nasal changes the person!

Note: a dot before a consonant is just a normal nasal consonant: संसार *sansār*, अंक *aṅk*.
tips: Hum while saying the vowel — if your nose vibrates, it's nasal.
Don't add an n or ng: गाउँ is 'gaa-ũ', not 'gaa-oong'.
Pinch your nose: an oral vowel sounds the same, a nasal one changes.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant (written as a conjunct: त्त, च्च, ट्ठ) is **held** for a moment before release, like the 'tt' in Italian 'gatto' or the join in English 'bookcase'. The vowel before it is short and clipped.

Doubling changes meaning: कति *kati* 'how much?' vs कत्ति *katti* '(not) at all'; पति *pati* 'husband' vs पत्ती *patti* 'tea leaves'.
tips: Pause on the consonant: 'kat-ti', 'bach-chā'.
Don't double by accident when a word has a single consonant (कति, पति).
Many numbers have doubles: सत्तरी 70, अट्ठाइस 28, छब्बीस 26.

pronunciation.title: e/o vs ai/au
pronunciation.body:
ए *e* and ओ *o* are **pure** vowels, as in Spanish: no gliding 'ay' or 'ow'. Keep your tongue and lips still: नेपाल is 'ne-pāl', not 'nay-pāl'; को *ko* is short and clean.

ऐ *ai* and औ *au* are **real glides** in Nepali — unlike Hindi, where they are often flattened. पैसा 'money' is 'pai-sā' (like 'pie'), नौ 'nine' is 'nau' (like 'now'). This makes several clear minimal pairs.
tips: e = French 'é', held steady.
o = Spanish 'o', no w at the end.
ai = 'eye' with a darker start; au = 'ow' in 'how'.

pronunciation.title: Questions, intonation and little particles
pronunciation.body:
A yes/no question in Nepali is just a statement with **rising intonation** at the end — no question word is needed: तपाईं नेपाली हो। 'You are Nepali.' → तपाईं नेपाली हो? 'Are you Nepali?' Stress is light and usually on the first syllable; don't stress the end of words English-style.

Spoken Nepali is full of small sentence-final particles that carry attitude:
**है** *hai* — friendly 'OK?/won't you?' (आउनुहोस् है 'do come, OK?')
**नि** *ni* — 'you know', 'what about…?' (तपाईं नि? 'And you?')
**त** *ta* — 'though, as for' (म त जान्छु 'I, for one, am going')
**न** *na* — softens commands (बस न 'do sit')
**र** *ra* at the end — surprise/doubt (हो र? 'Really?')
**हगि/हगी** *hagi* — Kathmandu 'right?'
tips: Raise your pitch on the last syllable for yes/no questions.
Use नि for 'and you?': म ठीक छु, तपाईं नि?
Add है to invitations and goodbyes to sound warm.
Question words (के, कहाँ…) usually go right before the verb, not first.

pronunciation.title: Spelling vs sound: other surprises
pronunciation.body:
A few more places where Nepali pronunciation departs from the letters:

**Weak h**: ह between vowels is often barely heard — बहिनी sounds like 'bo-i-ni', पहिलो 'pai-lo', कहिले 'kai-le'. We keep the h in romanization because careful speakers say it.
**ए and य**: initial य in a few words is said 'e' (यो *yo* 'this' stays yo, but एउटा *euṭā* 'one (thing)' is often heard 'yauṭā').
**ण** is just n; **ऋ** is ri (कृपया *kripayā*).
**Visarga** ः inside a word doubles the next sound (दुःख ≈ 'dukkha').
**-यो** after a consonant: गर्‍यो *garyo*, पर्‍यो *paryo* — the eyelash ra (र्‍) is pronounced as an ordinary r.
**English loans** follow Nepali sounds: z → j (जु *ju* 'zoo'), v → bh/b (भ्यान *bhyān* 'van'), f → ph (फोन *phon*), and initial 'st/sk' often gets an i- or e- (इस्कुल *iskul* 'school', colloquial).
tips: Don't over-pronounce h in the middle of words.
Expect loanwords to be 'Nepalified' — and copy that pronunciation; it's what people understand.
Spell-check with a dictionary; say it the way you hear it.
